beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about a strange, well-documented habit of AI models reading long documents. They're much better at using facts at the start or end than facts buried in the middle, even when nothing else about those facts is different.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01.

beats.narration_text: Give a model a short paragraph with one key fact, and it finds it every time. Give it a hundred-page document with that exact same fact buried on page fifty, and it can miss it completely, not because the fact is hard to understand, but because of where it happens to sit.
beats.new_visual_element: Two document icons side by side: a short one with a highlighted fact, and a long one with the same fact buried deep inside, both labeled with the same question

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical scenario — no real model named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the pattern researchers have repeatedly found. Picture a long context as a line: start, middle, end. Models are reliably better at using information near the two ends than information in the middle. It's not that the model can't technically see that part of the text. It's that attention across a long input isn't evenly distributed. The beginning and end get disproportionately more of it.
beats.new_visual_element: A long horizontal bar representing the context, with an attention-strength curve drawn over it, high at both ends, dipping in the middle

shot.note: Must show a real U-shaped curve diagram, not just assert it in narration. No specific numeric values on the curve.

beats.narration_text: Say you hand a model a long onboarding document and ask one specific question, and the answer is stated once, buried in the middle section. Ask the model, and it might miss it entirely, or guess at an answer that isn't actually in the text. The fact was right there. It just wasn't in a part of the document the model was reliably attending to.
beats.new_visual_element: A long document with the key fact highlighted in the middle section, the model's answer shown as wrong or 'not found', with a red marker on the middle of the attention curve

shot.note: The 'middle' position must be visually obvious, not just labeled.

beats.narration_text: Now move that exact same fact, same document, same question, just place it in the first paragraph or the last paragraph instead. Ask again, and the model gets it right. Nothing about the fact changed. Only where it sat in the document did.
beats.new_visual_element: The same document, same fact, now shown at the start or end, the model's answer now correct, a green marker on the end of the attention curve

shot.note: Same document, same fact, only position changes. Visually distinct resolution from B04 (green vs red marker).

beats.narration_text: Here's something to check today. Next time you're stuffing a long document or a long chat history into an AI model and asking it to use one specific detail, ask yourself: how long is the context? Where does the key fact actually sit? And would moving it toward the start or end change whether the model finds it? If the answer is yes, you've just found a real blind spot. Not a reason to distrust the model entirely, a reason to put the important part where it'll actually be seen.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3 questions as a checklist card

shot.note: Concrete action, not a restatement of B03 — should read as a checklist/task card.

beats.narration_text: A model that misses a fact buried in page fifty isn't failing to understand it. It's reading unevenly, and knowing that changes where you put the thing you actually need it to find.
